data.title: Police smash burglary ring that recruited illegal immigrants for 25 break-ins
data.description:
Hong Kong police have busted a burglary syndicate that recruited illegal immigrants and is believed to be behind at least 25 break-ins across the city in recent weeks, with stolen cash and valuables exceeding HK$3.6 million (US$458,773).
Six people aged 31 to 45 – five mainlanders and a local resident – were arrested in a Friday operation following a review of surveillance footage, police said.
Three of the mainland suspects, all men, were illegal immigrants. Another two – a couple – are believed to be the masterminds, who entered Hong Kong on two-way permits, travel documents issued by Beijing authorities for visits to the city or Macau.
A local man arrested in the operation acted as the group’s driver.
Acting chief inspector Ng See-hin, of the New Territories North Regional Crime Unit, said the syndicate had been active since late August, adding that it was allegedly linked to at least 25 burglaries at village houses and upscale homes in Yuen Long, Tuen Mun, Sheung Shui, Tai Po, Sai Kung, Ma On Shan and Aberdeen.
Ng said the group took advantage of recent long holidays and major festivals, when many residents were overseas or dining out.

“They have a clear division of labour,” he said. “The masterminds arranged for the mainland men to enter Hong Kong illegally and recruited a driver to transport them between target areas and their hideout.”
“They mainly target houses with lax security in quiet and secluded locations. They would pry open doors and windows while the owners were out dining or on holiday, or enter through unlocked doors and windows to steal gold jewellery, cash, watches and other valuables,” Ng added.
The total reported loss exceeded HK$3.6 million, with the largest single loss of about HK$600,000 at a property in Aberdeen.
“Some of the stolen property was recovered, including cash, jewellery and handbags. The total value is about HK$600,000,” he added, stressing that the force believed it had smashed the syndicate.
The six were still being detained for questioning on Saturday afternoon, according to Ng.
Ng also urged flat owners to remain vigilant and take simple precautions, such as locking windows and doors before leaving home.
“Most burglaries are opportunistic in nature. Burglars take immediate advantage of what they perceive to be lax security,” Ng said. “The public should avoid keeping too many valuables or large amounts of cash at home.”
Under the Theft Ordinance, the maximum penalty for burglary in Hong Kong is 14 years’ imprisonment.

data.title: ‘Cancer saved me’: Hong Kong survivor finds new purpose ahead of canoe challenge
data.description:
Thirty-one years ago, Hongkonger Raymond Lo Shu-yuen was diagnosed with stage four liver cancer and had a quarter of the organ removed.
Now 75, Lo said the illness, despite its physical and mental toll, had taught him invaluable lessons about ageing, health and making the most of life.
“I can say that the cancer itself saved me,” he said.
“Why? If I did not have this illness, I would not have changed my past lifestyle such as working hard like a dog, eating a lot of junk food, doing no exercise or workouts, keeping no pets and other lovely animals.”
Today, he is preparing to embark on a 65km (40 mile) solo canoeing challenge between Tung Chung and Ma Wan, aiming to raise funds for cancer patients and promote public health awareness.
Lo was diagnosed with liver cancer in 1995, at the age of 44. He said he had no symptoms until a routine physical check-up revealed a shadow on his liver. Subsequent CAT scans and blood tests confirmed the disease.
Though initially shocked, he said he quickly accepted the diagnosis. As a hepatitis B carrier, he faced an increased risk of serious liver complications, including cirrhosis and liver cancer.
Surgery successfully removed a quarter of his liver. During his recovery, he said he felt weak, lost his appetite and tired easily.
More than the physical pain, he said, he feared being unable to work and support his wife and three children – two sons and a daughter aged between 10 and 16.
“How could they survive without me? My wife was a housewife over 40 years of age and my children were all at school,” he said.
“I could overcome the physical pain in my whole body but could not manage economically for my family.”
To ease the stress, Lo left his job at a large logistics company, where he earned about HK$50,000 (US$6,371) a month, and joined a smaller firm for roughly half the salary.
It was then that he began making changes to cope with the illness – changes that later became lifelong habits.
He adopted a healthier, more balanced diet, eating vegetables and fruit he had grown himself, including sweet potatoes, pumpkins and papayas.
He also took in a dozen abandoned and stray dogs at his home in Sham Shek Tsuen, a village on Lantau Island.

“The activities kept me very busy and I had no time to think about my illness,” he said.
Alongside embracing a healthier lifestyle and developing a love of animals, Lo returned to canoeing, a hobby he had neglected for years.
He first took up the sport after finishing secondary school in 1971, when he joined the Auxiliary Medical Service to learn first aid, ambulance work and life-saving skills.
He volunteered as a canoe lifeguard for more than eight years in areas including Repulse Bay, Shek O, Big Wave Bay and Stanley. He also served as a lifeguard trainer and canoeing instructor for new members of the service.
He later left the service after the birth of his first child to spend more time with his family.
While looking for ways to stay healthy during his recovery from liver cancer, he returned to canoeing and fell in love with the sport all over again. He bought a second-hand canoe for about HK$6,000, which remains his favourite because of its manoeuvrability.
Lo said canoeing helped him stay focused and build self-confidence while enjoying nature.
“While canoeing, I can enjoy the sea, the landscape, the sky, the waves and currents,” he said. “I can canoe fast and slow. I don’t have a route to follow. I can move freely in the water.”
Lo now paddles at sea five days a week. He also works as a canoe instructor and has taught about 100 students.
Alongside his regular workouts and lessons, Lo has taken on a new task: preparing for a solo canoeing challenge in support of the Hong Kong Cancer Fund, to raise funds and awareness for cancer patients.
For the 65km endurance challenge, he will paddle non-stop for more than eight hours across open water between Tung Chung and Ma Wan.
Lo said he came up with the challenge after witnessing friends and colleagues die from various cancers in recent years. Some were in their forties or fifties and left families behind.
“Within the past 10 years, I have had a number of my friends and past colleagues who have died from various cancers,” he said.
“They did not take any medical examinations or check-ups. They thought they were healthy. They went on drinking alcohol, smoking cigarettes and eating a lot of junk food.”
He added that he hoped the challenge would raise public awareness of the importance of regular health check-ups and a healthy lifestyle.
Lo said potential difficulties on the solo journey included heavy rain, strong winds and, in particular, lightning.
He planned to set off in mid-October, depending on the weather.
“My main focus right now is that I must have a healthy body and live a vibrant, fulfilling life,” he said.
“Cancer has transformed me into someone who knows how to have fun and live life with enjoyment. It has built up another whole new life for me.”

data.title: ‘Balanced and acceptable’: labour chief defends helper wage rise amid criticism
data.description:
Hong Kong’s stronger economic performance over the past year was the reason for raising the monthly minimum wage for foreign domestic helpers by 2.35 per cent, the labour minister has said, amid disappointment from both unions and employers’ groups.
Defending the government’s decision to raise the monthly minimum wage to HK$5,220 (US$665), Secretary for Labour and Welfare Chris Sun Yuk-han said the government sought to keep the annual adjustment mechanism “balanced and acceptable”.
Speaking after a radio programme on Saturday, Sun said: “If you look back, the average annual increase has been between 2 per cent and 2.5 per cent for many years.
“If you look at the overall data, Hong Kong’s economic performance this year is better than last year, which everyone can see.”
The new wage level will apply to all contracts signed on or after Saturday. However, the government has kept the monthly food allowance for helpers who are not provided with free meals unchanged at HK$1,236.
The announcement drew criticism from both helpers’ groups and employers’ associations.
The Hong Kong Federation of Asian Domestic Workers Unions had earlier proposed raising the minimum wage to HK$6,670 and the food allowance to HK$2,770.
Employers, meanwhile, had called for a pay freeze, citing cost-of-living pressures on families that might reduce employment opportunities for helpers.
Last year, the government raised helpers’ minimum wage by 2.2 per cent, from HK$4,990 to HK$5,100, while leaving the food allowance unchanged.

Sun said authorities had considered data including inflation, employers’ income and Hong Kong’s overall economic performance when assessing this year’s increase.
“After considering this data, the government made a comprehensive decision on whether to adjust the minimum wage for that year, and if so, by how much,” he said, adding that a pay freeze had been implemented during the pandemic.
“We strive to ensure that the entire adjustment mechanism is balanced and acceptable to Hong Kong.
“I think this will ensure that Hong Kong continues to operate smoothly because many families need the help of foreign domestic helpers.”
About 380,000 foreign domestic helpers work in Hong Kong, most of them from the Philippines and Indonesia. While many earn the minimum wage, others command higher salaries depending on their experience and families’ caregiving needs.
According to the latest salary survey by HelperChoice, a Hong Kong-based recruitment platform, the average monthly wage for a helper was HK$5,559 in 2026, down 2.8 per cent from HK$5,722 a year earlier.
The survey, based on more than 1,000 job advertisements posted on the platform between September 2025 and August 2026, also found that salaries were highest on Hong Kong Island and lowest in the New Territories.

data.title: Prison term ‘karma’, says Hong Kong man freed after 26 years in Philippine jail
data.description:
On his 29th birthday, Hong Kong bartender Tang Lung-wai boarded a flight to the Philippines for a holiday that would change his life.
He ended up spending 26 years in jail in the country.
Now 55, Tang spent years fighting his drug-related charges, insisting that he had been framed. But he told the South China Morning Post that he did not view those lost decades solely through the lens of bitterness.
“At first, I felt a lot of resentment about being framed like that. But in the end, it’s no use holding onto so much resentment. Since you’re already in jail and since you cannot change what has already happened, you just have to change yourself to adapt to this environment,” he said.
Tang, who returned to Hong Kong on Tuesday after being released from prison, said he considered his 26 years behind bars “karma” for being a “b*****d” to his family, whom he had ignored, the friends he had betrayed and the girlfriends he had cheated on.
“What I learned in prison is how to be a proper human being,” he said.
“It is like heaven arranged for me to learn how to be a proper person. Once I have learned it, they let me out.”
Being able to walk out safe and sound, Tang considered himself to have repaid all his karmic debt.
‘Troubled kid’
Tang was arrested in Manila in July 2000 for possession of methamphetamine, also known as Ice, and remanded in custody. He was convicted more than a decade later, in 2011, and handed a life sentence, which in the Philippines can mean up to 40 years in prison.
A Manila court ruled in July that his sentence would be commuted in view of his good conduct. He was deported and returned home on Tuesday night.
Reflecting on his life behind bars, Tang said prison had changed him profoundly.
Growing up in a Kwai Chung public housing estate, Tang was the middle child in his family. As a teenager, he fell in with neighbourhood street gangs.
“People could tell right away that I was a troubled kid,” Tang recalled, stressing that he was never a triad member and had no criminal record in Hong Kong.
He fought for years to prove his innocence, arguing that he was not in the Philippines when surveillance related to the crime was carried out on June 1, 2000. He visited the country on June 19, 2000.

Tang said he believed he came to the attention of police when co-defendant Cheung Tai-on, a casino worker whom he knew through friends, picked him up at the airport. They travelled together for a few days.
He recalled that Cheung later admitted to telling police his whereabouts after he himself was arrested.
On July 18, police pulled Tang from a taxi outside his hotel in Manila. He was taken to a police station where he claimed he was beaten up and extorted for money in exchange for his release.
Police then placed him in a flat in Quezon City, Metro Manila, with other co-defendants and staged a raid, finding 8kg of Ice inside, he said. He said they were forced to admit the crime at gunpoint.
Tang recalled he was furious with Cheung and assaulted him several times while they were remanded in a police cell. But as time passed, he forgave him. Cheung once took the blame for him after he was caught keeping a mobile phone, a banned item in prison, and was kept in solitary confinement for a month.
Cheung died of a heart attack in prison in 2016. “When he died, I could not believe I cried. I really cried. I think it’s a pity,” he said.
Low profile for survival
Tang spent 11 years in custody before he was convicted. He was remanded for eight months in a police cell before he was sent to Quezon City Jail – infamous for overcrowding and poor living conditions – where he said he spent his worst few years.
He said the prison was like a small community with shops, restaurants and wet markets operated by inmates, as well as gyms, churches and hospitals.
“Never use a Hong Kong perspective to think about the Philippines,” he said, adding that the rich could even build houses inside the prison. “You can live a different life depending on how much you have in your pocket.”
At first he had no money to secure a bed from the inmate leader and slept on the ground, sometimes by a drain or outside a toilet, jostling with other prisoners, he said. Conditions were so bad that he caught a skin disease.
“I was always starving,” he said, as prison only served small pieces of meat, a small bowl of rice and some bread.

“I was so poor that I had no money to buy toothpaste,” Tang recalled, adding that he used his fingers to rub salt on his teeth to clean them.
He earned extra food by washing clothes for wealthier Chinese inmates, looking after their children, who were allowed to stay in prison during family visits, and helping out in restaurants.
Tang said he saw gang fights and murders inside the prison and to survive he kept a low profile. “Some prison officers did not know my name after all these 26 years,” he said.
He began writing letters to appeal for help in 2003. As a British National (Overseas) passport holder, he first wrote to the British embassy in Manila. “It took me seven hours to write. There was no AI. I just looked it up in the dictionary,” he said.
He later received allowances of 10,000 pesos every three months from the embassy. He also called the Hong Kong Immigration Department for help.
Into prison routine
After Tang was convicted in 2011, he was transferred to the notorious New Bilibid Prison in Manila.
Following an appeal for help, he received around HK$10,000 in donations. He shared some with Cheung, and spent 10,500 pesos to buy himself a 40 sq ft room with a bed from an inmate leader.
He spent the remaining 6,500 pesos to buy his first smartphone and secretly kept it.
Tang used his smartphone to learn how to use social media and began writing articles on Facebook about his life in prison.
He later published two books, which earned him public attention and donations from readers. However, he received two years of solitary confinement as punishment in 2018.
Tang said his prison life over the past few years had been quite routine. He lived in a large cell with 70 other foreigners.

Waking up at 10am, he hit the gym in the morning and then went to the market to buy food, paid for by other prisoners, and prepared lunch for them. He then took a nap and went jogging in the afternoon. After preparing dinner for other inmates, he played on his mobile phone.
Tang said that he had picked up conversational Tagalog but could not fully follow the television news.
Back in Hong Kong, apart from getting a driving licence to make a living, Tang said he also wanted to offer help to troubled youth and obtain a first aid certificate so that he could rescue anyone in an emergency. He also plans to write a third book to record his experiences and anecdotes from prison.
“Hong Kong people have helped me a lot. I also wish to contribute to this society,” he said.
While he had lost the prime years of his life in which he might have had his own family, Tang said he would just go with the flow.
“After these 26 years, there may be something even worse in my life that lies ahead. I don’t know. But I will be stronger in adversity,” he said.

data.title: More Chinese banks likely to adopt AI rules after Ping An move: analysts
data.description:
After Ping An Bank became the first listed Chinese lender to formally adopt rules governing its use of artificial intelligence, analysts said more mainland institutions were likely to follow, with the move setting an early benchmark for how far the sector can go in applying the technology.
The Shenzhen-listed bank said in a filing on Wednesday that its board had approved AI management measures, following a regulatory push for banks to strengthen oversight of AI use. The full rules have not been made public.
No other listed bank in mainland China had announced similar measures, according to comments Ping An Bank recently gave to domestic media outlets.
The lender also said its board’s strategy committee would oversee AI-related matters, with checks at “every stage of development and use” and mechanisms for data security, algorithm risk, ethics review and responsibility tracing. It would classify AI risks by level and fold them into an overall risk-management system.
The measures implement guidelines issued in June by the National Financial Regulatory Administration. These guidelines hold banks and insurers responsible for the AI systems they use and require boards to establish oversight mechanisms.
The bank had rolled out more than 450 large-model AI use cases by the end of June, in areas including marketing, investment advice, compliance and risk control, according to its interim report.
More banks in China and globally will move towards this direction
Gary Ng, Natixis
Several other banks were working to implement the guidelines and expected to issue similar governance rules, Shanghai-based financial news agency Cailian Press reported. All 42 A-share listed banks mentioned AI in their interim reports this year, it added.
Kenny Tang Sing-hing, chairman of the Hong Kong Institute of Financial Analysts and Professional Commentators, said the announcement provided limited detail, including how the technology would be deployed in practice.
“But I believe this is the future trend for financial institutions,” he said.
Given the range of mainland regulations involved, it would take time to see how far regulators were prepared to allow banks to expand their use of AI, Tang added.
Gary Ng, senior economist for the Asia-Pacific region at Natixis, said AI adoption “must come with governance, particularly in finance, where the protection of customers and financial stability” were critical.
“More banks in China and globally will move towards this direction,” Ng added.
The development comes as Hong Kong officials urge local financial institutions to prepare for a new wave of autonomous AI systems and position the city as a hub for international compliance standards.
Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po wrote in his weekly blog on Sunday that the city could offer “trusted solutions” in areas including AI model training, cross-border data flows, privacy protection and dispute resolution.
He cited the city’s common law system, internationally connected standards and professional services sector as key advantages.
In March, Hong Kong’s financial regulators expanded a supervised sandbox for generative AI, originally launched for banks in 2024, to include the securities, insurance and pensions sectors.
Tang said many Hong Kong banks and insurers had already adopted AI to reduce operating expenses, particularly compliance-related costs.
Ng said Hong Kong could be “a perfect place to test and apply the standards of different jurisdictions in an increasingly fragmented world”.

data.title: ‘Better than expected’: 73,800 subdivided flats apply for 3-year grace period
data.description:
More than 73,000 subdivided flats in Hong Kong have applied for a three-year grace period to meet the government’s minimum standards, a figure the housing chief has described as “better than expected”.
Secretary for Housing Winnie Ho Wing-yin said on Saturday that authorities received around 73,800 applications during the “early bird” registration phase under the Basic Housing Unit Ordinance, which closed on August 31.
The tally represented nearly 70 per cent of the city’s estimated 110,000 subdivided flats, with 42 already certified as compliant, Ho told a radio programme.
“The progress is better than I expected,” she said. “We expect that as we gradually enter the three-year grace period, as people become familiar with the certification process and find suitable renovation companies and professionals to handle it, the certification numbers will rise.”
Ho urged remaining landlords to register before the grace period began next March.
“We hope all landlords will register first, regardless of what you decide to do in the future, whether you continue operating or not, or rectify the current situation to make it compliant,” she said.
Under Hong Kong’s inaugural five-year plan, authorities aim to eliminate substandard subdivided flats in residential buildings by 2030 by boosting supply and cutting public housing waiting times.

Landlords who applied between March and August qualified for a waiver of HK$3,000 (US$382) in recognition fees per subdivided flat until February 2029.
A second six-month registration round, offering smaller fee discounts, is now under way and will complete the overall one-year application period.
From March next year, only subdivided flats that meet minimum requirements and are certified as “basic housing units” may be legally leased, except for those covered by the grace period.
The grace period runs from March 2027 to February 2030, giving landlords time to refurbish and certify their properties.
Landlords must bear renovation and certification costs and pay the government HK$3,000 per subdivided flat for recognition as basic housing units.
On the same programme, Ho revealed that 90.6 per cent of Wang Fuk Court owners had returned signed letters accepting the government’s buy-back offer.
She spoke three days after the first batch of about 100 homeowners selected their replacement flats earlier this week.

Following last November’s fire at Wang Fuk Court, authorities launched a HK$7.8 billion plan to buy back flats at the eight-block subsidised housing estate.
Under the scheme, participants can use the cash compensation to purchase a flat on the private market or join a special sales exercise to buy new subsidised housing under the government’s “flat-for-flat” arrangement.
Ho said a dedicated explanation team accompanied around 30 households daily, assisting them through the process, as many comprised elderly residents who needed time to consult their families.
Public housing estates with faster completion times, such as those in Kowloon Bay and Fanling, proved popular as residents wanted to move into their new homes as soon as possible, she added.
Ho said the remaining 10 per cent of owners who had not signed sale and purchase agreements should complete the process by October 15.
“If they ultimately decide not to sign a contract with us, we will consider it a refusal to sell,” she said, adding that they would be grouped with the 13 households that did not sign letters accepting the acquisition offer.
“We will handle these cases later. For example, we might need to consider legislation to address this.”

data.title: Mainland Chinese arrivals in first 2 days of ‘golden week’ holiday top 2018 total
data.description:
Mainland Chinese visitor arrivals in Hong Kong during the first two days of the National Day “golden week” surpassed the pre-pandemic total for the same period in 2018, as the tourism chief expressed confidence that the city would reach its annual target of 53.8 million visitors earlier than expected.
The city recorded 511,311 arrivals from the mainland on Thursday and Friday, according to Immigration Department figures, edging past the 508,578 recorded during the same period in 2018.
The first day of the holiday drew 277,304 mainland visitors, up from 247,626 on the opening day in 2018. The second day welcomed 234,007, compared with 260,952 that year.
Secretary for Culture, Sports and Tourism Rosanna Law Shuk-pui said on Saturday that mainland arrivals on the first day had surpassed the pre-pandemic high, with many visitors also arriving early for the Mid-Autumn Festival.

“Visitor numbers over the Mid-Autumn Festival weekend rose 28 per cent, so if the golden week still posts a 5 per cent increase on top of that, it is actually quite a lot,” she said.
Asked whether the city would reach its 53.8 million visitor target ahead of schedule, Law said she was very confident despite the challenges posed by global conditions.
“The global conditions, particularly in Southeast Asia, do pose challenges, as short-haul travellers’ willingness to spend and to visit Hong Kong has been affected by high airfares overall,” she said.
The 53.8 million target, set by the government at the start of the year, represents an 8 per cent increase on the 49.89 million arrivals recorded in 2025.
Law said the authorities would also “go out more” to understand travellers’ preferences. She said she hoped to return to markets such as Southeast Asia to step up promotion once global conditions stabilised.
She added that events such as the Victoria Park Mid-Autumn lantern carnival, organised by the Tourism Board and the retail and catering sectors, had drawn a strong response and showcased the city’s East-meets-West appeal.

data.title: Hong Kong Airport Authority to reshape 11 Skies as a high-end tourism landmark
data.description:
The Airport Authority will reposition the 11 Skies commercial project after taking it over next April, with the government expecting it to become a high-end tourism landmark with minimal public investment, the transport chief has said.
Speaking for the first time since developer New World Development (NWD) announced on Wednesday that it would return the 11 Skies project to the authority next April, Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan said on Saturday that the two sides had reached an agreement on commercial and contractual principles.
“From the government perspective, we are pleased and welcome to see both sides trying to resolve this matter as far as practicable,” she told a radio programme.
The handover includes an entertainment complex and three office towers. Debt-ridden New World will provide more than HK$3 billion (US$382.3 million) in cash or equivalents, following major losses.
On Wednesday, the authority said it was taking forward the project “full steam ahead” and aimed to create a unique entertainment hub that would open in the 2028-29 financial year.
Chan said the authority would align the project with its Airport City development, with the aim of making 11 Skies a core landmark for high-end tourism activities.
Airport City is a development blueprint to expand Hong Kong International Airport as a key aviation hub while creating a new destination for business and leisure.
“The agreement allows the Airport Authority to set a clear road map and timetable to take over and reposition the project,” she said.
“We expect the authority to turn the project into a core landmark for high-end aviation, luxury retail, arts and culture, tourism and water sports like yachting.”

She added that a dedicated team would upgrade the offices, shops and restaurants in the original 11 Skies plan, adding more experiential activities for passengers, particularly those in transit.
Chan said the authority would align the project with the opening of Airport Terminal 2 at the end of 2027 and the completion of AsiaWorld-Expo Phase 2 in 2028, allowing visitors to enjoy concerts. The project would also integrate with autonomous vehicles to provide smart transport through a “SkyCity Corridor” linking the Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macau Bridge.
“The project would provide seamless connections for passengers from around the world. Travellers can experience Hong Kong’s business, entertainment, dining and tourism without leaving the airport area,” she said.
She added that the authority also planned to invite expressions of interest next year for two future tenders: an art storage facility and a marina bay in Airport City.
On government investment in the project, Chan said that under Hong Kong’s five-year plan, the government would oversee the authority’s Airport City development to ensure it required minimal public investment.
“The authority must conduct careful commercial operational estimates including calculating its rate of return for each item to keep its own direct investment to a minimum. We also hope to attract investors into the project which will be put into tender for every smaller item,” she said.
The 11 Skies project was intended to complement the authority’s plan to develop Skytopia, a HK$100 billion landmark surrounding Hong Kong International Airport, with commercial, cultural, leisure and entertainment elements.
The HK$20 billion 11 Skies development was originally expected to include three grade A office towers totalling 52,955 square metres (570,000 square feet), alongside about 247,000 square metres of retail and dining space – 70 per cent of the entire project.

data.title: Exclusive|Hong Kong to relax ad rules for broadcasters to boost business edge, minister says
data.description:
Hong Kong authorities plan to relax restrictions on indirect advertising for broadcasters amid fierce competition from online and streaming media, the commerce minister has told the South China Morning Post.
In a wide-ranging exclusive interview, Secretary for Commerce and Economic Development Algernon Yau Ying-wah said many broadcast operators had requested to review the Generic Codes of Practice for Television to improve the business environment, and the government had responded.
“They’re saying that the competition from other media is very strong, and it’s very difficult for them to survive, and then we have to be up market and then match the practice internationally,” Yau said on Thursday.
In the annual policy address released last month, the government pledged to review the code to ensure that regulations keep pace with the times and that diversified, quality programmes were broadcast, expanding the reach of the ‘Hong Kong Brand’ in the Asia-Pacific region.
Yau said the review would include examining the current restrictions on how much English and Putonghua programmes could be broadcast, as well as indirect advertisements during TV programmes.
“Now it’s very restrictive. Even though you are drinking a can of soda drink, you cannot have their logo, they have to cover it up. But we are going to relax that,” he said.

Yau also said other advertising restrictions could be relaxed in the future, such as for the promotion of alcohol.
His bureau would discuss with other bureaus how to ensure the changes did not have any negative impact on the public, while at the same time giving the broadcasting industry more flexibility and freedom.
“[Their] life is getting more difficult with more online [media], streaming, and all these are not under very stringent control, not just by Hong Kong, internationally. No country is having very, very effective rules controlling streaming and online media,” he said.
Asked if the government had any plans to place restrictions on online and streaming media, Yau said it was very difficult to control the content being published online and other jurisdictions faced the same challenge.
The minister said the bureau would aim to conduct a consultation in the last quarter of this year and produce recommendations next year.
He said the review process would likely extend beyond the current government’s term, but the five-year plan could ensure policy continuity.
“I don’t see any problem at all if there’s a change of the government or government officials in the next term,” he said.
The review would be a “total review with all media” and not just broadcasting.
“The whole idea in the policy address is to facilitate the media and the creative industry, like TV, film, etc, so that they can have a new ecosystem in doing business,” he said.

The government had earlier proposed a legal amendment to protect copyrighted works from being used to train artificial intelligence (AI) models.
Yau said it would be “premature” at this moment to amend the Copyright Ordinance in view of the rapid development of AI and the different views received during public consultation. Any legal amendment would be “reviewed at the right time”.
“It’s premature, too early. Even though we change it, it will have to be changed tomorrow and then the day after tomorrow. Because AI is evolving too quickly. You don’t know what is going to happen tomorrow,” he said.
“Two mega countries having AI are the United States and China. And if both of them are going to have some amendment changes and that will be followed by other countries and economies, then we can have a look to see whether it is practical and applicable to Hong Kong as well,” he said.
Yau said the government would issue guidelines by the end of this year if possible for business sectors and individuals on how to develop AI, with details to be discussed with the sector.

data.title: Hongkongers lose HK$220 million to customer service scams in August
data.description:
Scams involving fraudsters posing as customer service officers caused losses of over HK$220 million (US$28.2 million) in August in Hong Kong, more than triple the monthly average in the first seven months of the year, police have said.
The police force also warned that scammers had shifted their modus operandi from using phishing links to taking real-time control of victims through direct calls and screen sharing, or tricking them into installing a malicious app that turned mobile phones into a credit card reader.
Hong Kong recorded 29,670 scam cases in the first eight months of 2026, up 4.5 per cent from 28,379 in the same period a year earlier, with losses rising by 3.8 per cent to HK$5.2 billion.
About 17 per cent, or around 5,000 cases, were customer service scams, which incurred total losses of nearly HK$700 million.
The number of such scams soared from a monthly average of about 480 in the first seven months to more than 1,680 in August. Losses exceeded HK$220 million in August, more than triple the monthly average of the previous seven months.

More than 1,600 cases in August involved scammers making phone calls and posing as customer service staff from banks, logistics firms and telecoms companies. The remaining 80 cases involved message-based scams.
Superintendent Rachel Hui Yee-wai of the cybersecurity and technology crime bureau said the fraudsters’ shift away from phishing links reflected the evolution of scams as the public grew wary of such tricks.
“They no longer just send you a link. They call you directly, and instantly they are working on your emotions,” she said.
“If they want to take everything in your account, they have to operate with you, step by step, in real time. When you get stuck, they guide you on the spot, even via screen sharing. That gives them far greater control over the victim than a link ever could.”
She urged the public to verify any customer service claim through official channels found independently – never through contact details provided by the caller.
Chief Inspector Wong Cheung-hing of the bureau said police had identified two new methods used by scammers.
In the first, victims are tricked into downloading a malicious application on their phone and then instructed to enable near-field communication (NFC), the technology behind contactless payments, and tap their credit cards on the phones for “verification” or “refund” purposes. They unknowingly hand over their card data, after which fraudulent transactions follow.
“When the victim notices unauthorised transactions and questions them, the scammer claims a refund is due and asks them to tap the card again, completing a second theft,” Wong said.
The second method involves scammers posing as courier staff who claim a parcel cannot be delivered and that compensation is due. They then guide victims to log in to their own online banking and add the scammer’s account as a new payee.
Claiming the account has to be verified, the scammer gives the victims a string of digits as a “verification code” and tells them to enter it into the payment amount field, sending the sum to the fraudster’s account.


Police cited two cases in August with combined losses of nearly HK$8 million. In one case, a 74-year-old businessman, who received a phishing text impersonating a courier firm, called the customer service number provided and gave his account details, losing HK$3.4 million.
In the other case, a 53-year-old housewife returned a call from scammers posing as Taobao customer service staff who promised her compensation for “a damaged parcel”.
After logging into a fake website and her online banking account, she added a scammer-controlled account as a payee and entered a “verification code” in the amount field, transferring HK$4.46 million.
In response to the rising losses, police said they had stepped up action on three fronts: taking down scam websites and their operators; intercepting bulk scam texts at the telecoms level; and arresting those who laundered the proceeds.
More than 1,500 fake sender IDs had been blocked in the first eight months of the year, while the force’s Scameter app logged over 500,000 public scam reports during the same period, more than 40,000 of them courier-related.
On the industry side, major courier firm SF Express said it had stopped sending customer notifications by SMS in 2025, pushing all updates through its official app instead.
Chun Yuk-ying, head of public affairs and communications at SF Express, said the switch had cut the firm’s scam victimisation rate from 5.03 per cent to 0.65 per cent.

data.title: Trump wants to stamp out the term ‘artificial intelligence’. Why?
data.description:
US President Donald Trump wants to retire one of the technology sector’s most recognisable acronyms, arguing that the term “artificial intelligence”, or AI, is no longer fit for purpose.
On Tuesday, Trump signed an executive order directing US federal agencies to replace “artificial intelligence” and “AI” with “super intelligence” and “SI” in official communications and non-statutory documents. He also instructed the White House science adviser to draft a new federal definition.
The move formalises a rebrand Trump launched at the United Nations General Assembly last week, where he claimed calling the technology “artificial” made it sound “fake”.
The change has sparked debate and put US tech leaders in an awkward position. SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk caught himself using the old term during a recent appearance with Trump, before correcting himself: “SI, pardon me.”
Meanwhile, California Governor Gavin Newsom pushed back on Wednesday, ordering state agencies to stick with “AI”.
Does this semantic tussle signal a deeper shift in how Washington views a technology central to the US-China rivalry?
Why the name change?
The White House argued frontier systems had moved beyond merely imitating or automating aspects of human intelligence, making “super intelligence” a better reflection of their growing capabilities and potential.
The shift aligns with Trump’s broader push to accelerate American tech development. At the UN, he rejected calls to slow progress, arguing he would not “stifle growth” in an industry that could eclipse the Industrial Revolution in terms of its impact.
This contrasts with recent calls from AI industry leaders – including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Musk – to pace model development over safety concerns. Instead, Trump cast technological leadership as a global race the US could not afford to lose to China.


The rebrand follows Trump’s summit in Washington with Chinese President Xi Jinping, where both nations agreed to establish a dialogue and communication channel for AI-related incidents. Trump said he discussed his preferred “super intelligence” phrasing with Xi.
Analysts view the shift as an attempt to control the narrative. Su Lian Jye, chief analyst at Omdia, said the rebrand could be seen as a way to “introduce a new phase in AI development” to project American dominance.
Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution, noted that “branding and optics matter a lot” to Trump, who likely wanted to hype the technology and tie it to his legacy.
Does the terminology matter?
Industry observers expect limited practical impact – and warn the move could create confusion.
Chan said the shift was unlikely to change public attitudes towards AI, warning it might actually “heighten some people’s perception of risk and fear”. Su noted that while consumer adoption was unlikely to shift, it could “create more confusion around standardisation and governance”.
Complicating matters, “superintelligence” already has an established technical definition, generally referring to systems surpassing human capabilities across all domain tasks. For instance, Meta Platforms rebranded its division to Meta Superintelligence Labs last year.
Reactions among tech and political leaders have been mixed.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang backed the move, writing on X that “super intelligence offers an extraordinary opportunity to advance discovery, productivity, security, health and prosperity”.
California Governor Newsom warned the rebrand could distract from safety risks and signed an order stating that the move could not hide an “impotent and craven failure to address well-documented emerging security and safety risks”.
How has China reacted?
Beijing has approached the rebrand with caution. China’s foreign ministry said it “respects” Washington’s choice while continuing to use the term “artificial intelligence”.
Su noted that adopting terms like “super” would be “very out of character” for China, which has favoured a pragmatic tech approach.
Wang Zichen, deputy secretary general at the Beijing-based Centre for China and Globalisation, said many in China were likely to view the rebrand as an “idiosyncratic preference” of Trump that added no value to the US-China debate.
However, Wang noted that “Beijing naturally has reason to take [Trump’s] preferred wording seriously and accommodate it diplomatically”.

data.title: McDonald’s sells Hong Kong shop for US$15.3 million as ‘old money’ returns
data.description:
As “long-dormant old money” steps back into Hong Kong’s retail property market, McDonald’s has sold the property housing its first New Territories restaurant for HK$120 million (US$15.3 million), extending its year-long sell-down of self-owned shops.
The property at 10-22 Tsuen Wan Market Street, spanning the ground floor to the second floor, was sold to Keen Charm Holdings (HK) Limited, with the agreement for sale signed on August 31, according to the Land Registry.
Company Registry listed Ngan Chi-hung, Ngan Chi-wai and Ngan Tuet-ching as directors of the purchasing vehicle.
They are reportedly identified as family members behind a Hong Kong toy manufacturer, May Cheong Group. The family-owned company was founded in 1967 in a small factory in Hong Kong by P.Y. Ngan and Y.C. Ngan, according to its website. The group did not respond to a request for comment.
Land Registry records show McDonald’s Restaurants (Hong Kong) Limited bought the property for HK$8 million in 1987, giving the company a HK$112 million gain, or a 14-fold return, on the sale.
Shop values in Hong Kong have come under pressure in recent years as the pandemic and shifts in consumer spending have weighed on retail demand, particularly in traditional shopping areas.
Eunice Tang, executive director of capital markets at JLL, which is marketing some of the McDonald’s shops, said the sales had attracted interest from “long-dormant old money” and “high-net-worth buyers” seeking prime retail properties backed by blue-chip tenants.
“[The interest] is driven largely by the shops’ reputable tenants and extended lease commitments,” Tang said.
The restaurant opened in 1978 as the first McDonald’s outlet in the New Territories and the chain’s 11th in Hong Kong. McDonald’s now operates 11 outlets in Tsuen Wan. It will continue operating from the property under a 20-year lease that runs through December 2036, according to the Land Registry.
The sale comes as McDonald’s continues to monetise properties accumulated over decades of expansion. The company initially planned to sell all 23 of its self-owned shops in Hong Kong, with the portfolio valued at about HK$3 billion.
Since launching the disposal programme in July last year, it has sold at least 13 properties for about HK$1.2 billion, including the latest Tsuen Wan transaction, according to South China Morning Post calculations and Land Registry records.
The sales come as transactions for retail properties valued above HK$50 million have remained sluggish in Hong Kong. Industry representatives have estimated that shop mortgage lending has fallen to about 20 per cent of its peak. Landlords have said banks are increasingly reluctant to lend against retail properties, leaving potential buyers unable to secure financing.

data.title: DeepSeek effect? How China’s quant funds thrive amid tight regulatory scrutinyStrong returns are attracting investors to quant funds, with DeepSeek highlighting the sector’s potential role in China’s
data.description:
China’s quantitative investing sector has added 18 new members to the ranks of funds managing more than 10 billion yuan (US$1.5 billion) in assets this year, underlining the industry’s ability to generate competitive returns despite a tight regulatory environment.
The firms were among 159 Chinese hedge funds overseeing more than 10 billion yuan each, according to financial news agency Cailian Press. Their growth has been fuelled by technology-driven momentum in the world’s second-largest stock market.
Among the latest entrants to the club were AXQ Capital, Hopeseek Fund and Huanian Fund, according to financial data provider Wind.
“Many quant funds are now doing exceptionally well,” said Christopher Beddor, deputy China research director at economic research firm Gavekal Dragonomics.
“China’s onshore equity market is less sophisticated than major global markets,” Beddor said. “[That means] quant funds can often generate solid returns by deploying systematic trading strategies that were first developed abroad.”
Amid China’s push towards fiscal self-reliance, quant funds helped improve the efficiency of the onshore equity market, according to Beddor.
More Chinese investors are moving into financial assets due to low deposit rates and weak real estate performance
Gary Ng, Natixis
Gary Ng, economist at investment bank Natixis, said Chinese investors increasingly viewed hedge funds favourably.
“More Chinese investors are moving into financial assets due to low deposit rates and weak real estate performance,” he said.
Quant funds are also becoming more accessible. Chinese brokerages, such as Sinolink Securities and Shenwan Hongyuan Securities, have started promoting quant trading services through their mobile apps, allowing eligible investors to apply for access to China’s quant trading platforms.
Despite their competitive returns, China’s quant funds operated in “a very tricky regulatory environment”, Beddor said.
Even though “China’s financial regulators are much more invested in market outcomes than regulators in other major markets,” they “can and do crack down on quant funds if they feel those firms may be contributing to market volatility”, said Beddor.
While the rise of the 18 quant funds highlighted the sector’s success, the “tighter regulatory regime” introduced in late 2024 had “clearly crimped some funds at the margin”, Beddor said.
He pointed to DeepSeek, backed by Chinese quant fund High-Flyer, as a possible turning point in how policymakers viewed quant funds.
“DeepSeek was created by a fund, not a traditional tech company,” he said. “Its breakthrough was the first time that policymakers seemed to have realised the fund industry could play a serious role in technological development.”
The 18 quant funds took an average of 8.4 years to surpass the 10 billion yuan assets-under-management mark, although five reached the milestone in less than five years.
China’s discretionary-fund sector has also expanded, with 18 funds crossing the 10 billion yuan asset threshold this year as of late September, according to Cailian Press.
Chinese private securities investment funds, including but not limited to quant funds and discretionary funds, managed more than 9 trillion yuan in assets as of the end of August, according to the Asset Management Association of China.

data.title: Off-duty senior ambulanceman dies after abseiling fall on Kowloon Peak
data.description:
An off-duty senior ambulanceman has died after falling from a cliff while abseiling in Hong Kong.
The Fire Services Department said on Friday that it had received a report at 2.33pm that a man had fallen from Kowloon Peak in Wong Tai Sin while abseiling.
Rescuers and a government helicopter searched the area and found an unconscious man at a nearby cliff. Another man with minor injuries was found on a nearby trail.
The department mobilised its mountain and high-angle rescue teams during the search and a drone was also deployed.
Both men were airlifted to Pamela Youde Nethersole Eastern Hospital in Chai Wan for treatment. The unconscious man was later pronounced dead.
The department confirmed the two men were both off-duty senior ambulancemen.
“The department expressed its utmost sadness over the death of its member and extended condolences to his family members,” a spokesman said, adding that it would provide all possible help.

data.title: 2 Hongkongers held in Philippines for months after prison terms end
data.description:
The Chinese embassy in Manila has expressed concern over the cases of two Hongkongers who have remained in custody in the Philippines for months despite being discharged from prison, according to the Immigration Department.
The department confirmed on Friday night that it was handling the two cases following an appeal from a former lawmaker and a Hong Kong man who returned to the city on Tuesday after serving 26 years in a Philippine prison for drug offences.
The returned Hongkonger, Tang Lung-wai, met the two residents, surnamed Cheung and Ng, in prison. He said he had also been held for weeks at the same immigration facility in the country as the pair while he waited to be deported.
Tang said Cheung and Ng were both arrested over drug-related offences in 2000 and 2001 and had completed their jail terms.
The Philippines Bureau of Immigration issued deportation orders, seen by the South China Morning Post, to Cheung and Ng in March and June, respectively. Tang said the pair were still waiting to complete their identity confirmation process.
Tang said Cheung had his fingerprints taken for the first time after waiting for six months. Ng had his fingerprints taken six or seven times, but they had not been accepted.
Ng and Cheung both received 40-year jail sentences. Ng was supposed to have been discharged in January 2025 and Cheung in January this year. However, their transfers to immigration facilities were also delayed.

Former lawmaker Paul Tse Wai-chun, who had been helping Tang for years, also appealed on Facebook for an early return of both of them.
“I hope that the [Hong Kong] government and other lawmakers will continue to pay attention and help them return as soon as possible,” he said.
The Immigration Department was actively following up on two cases involving residents who had completed their sentences in the Philippines and required repatriation to Hong Kong, a spokesman said.
He said the department would provide feasible help and had been liaising on the cases with the Office of the Commissioner of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Chinese embassy in the Philippines, including verifying the identities of the individuals and issuing entry permit documents for their return.
“The [Chinese] embassy in the Philippines has also expressed concern over the relevant cases and will continue to liaise with the Philippine authorities to coordinate the relevant repatriation arrangements,” he said.
The department said the Hong Kong government had always attached great importance to cases involving residents detained or imprisoned outside the city, paying close attention to their legitimate rights and interests and striving to provide them with help.
Tang was convicted of drug possession in 2011 and handed a life sentence, which in the Philippines amounts to a maximum of 40 years in prison.
A Manila court ruled in July that Tang’s sentence would be commuted in view of his good conduct and he was ordered to be released and deported immediately.
Tang waited three weeks in the immigration facilities before he was deported on Tuesday after his family appealed to the Hong Kong government for help.

data.title: Hong Kong could overtake London as top arbitration hub in decade: Bar Association head
data.description:
Hong Kong could dethrone London as the top choice for arbitration within the next decade given the Asian city’s status as a global fundraising capital for businesses in mainland China and beyond, the head of the Bar Association has said.
Jose-Antonio Maurellet, chairman of the Hong Kong Bar Association, told the South China Morning Post on Friday that the city had enjoyed rapid growth in arbitration work, with high-stakes cases attracting elite international legal talent.
Hong Kong tied with Singapore as the second-most preferred arbitration seat globally last year in a survey by Queen Mary University of London, trailing only the British capital.
The total amount in dispute in arbitration cases administered by the Hong Kong International Arbitration Centre, the city’s oldest arbitration body, last year was HK$117.7 billion (US$15 billion).

Maurellet said Hong Kong could overtake London’s arbitration crown in less than 10 years as the city was increasingly chosen to resolve high-value disputes linked to its role as an international capital-raising hub.
“What we see in Hong Kong actually is more and more big players from the United States or even London acting for clients in Hong Kong,” Maurellet said.
“It means we get to cross swords with the best from elsewhere.”
The association chief made the remarks after attending a ceremony in London to mark the opening of the legal year in England and Wales.
More than 100 senior figures from legal organisations from over 40 jurisdictions worldwide attended the event at Westminster Abbey on Thursday.
Maurellet explained that a key factor driving overseas interest in Hong Kong’s arbitration services was the international composition of the city’s arbitrators.

The senior counsel said one-third of arbitrators at the Hong Kong International Arbitration Centre hailed from other common law jurisdictions such as England, Australia and New Zealand.
However, Maurellet acknowledged that some foreign practitioners still viewed Hong Kong primarily as a forum for China-related disputes.
“They’re quite interested in basically asking, well, is it all about China?” he said.
Maurellet stressed that the broader international scope of the city’s arbitration caseload should be highlighted to build global confidence.
“Although a big part of the business is China-related, and we all know the advantages of being bilingual, there’s also, as the pie grows bigger, a part of that pie is available for international lawyers,” he said.
He added: “We also have interesting new markets like Brazil, Indonesia and the United Arab Emirates, and I think that really raises quite a lot of interest.”
Maurellet said he had received more inquiries than anticipated regarding the Hong Kong-headquartered International Organisation for Mediation, with lawyers showing keen interest in its mandate to resolve interstate conflicts and asking how to join as mediators.
“I think for certain jurisdictions, which for whatever cultural or geographical reasons in the past would not have gone to the more traditional historical places where this sort of work was done, I think Hong Kong opens up one more option, so I think it’s seen extremely positively,” he said.

data.title: Cutting New World ties over 11 Skies averts ‘lose-lose’ deal: Airport Authority
data.description:
The Airport Authority has averted a “lose-lose situation” by terminating a nearly 50-year contract with Hong Kong developer New World Development for the 11 Skies commercial project, with most facilities set to open in 2028, the statutory body’s directors have said.
Julian Lee Pui-hang, the authority’s executive director for finance, said on Friday that the organisation could no longer work with a debt-ridden partner on the ambitious development and that the project needed to be brought forward.
He said the authority could adopt a “technical solution” of taking New World to court for failing to deliver the project, but it would come with pitfalls.
“We could have sought a settlement in court, but it sacrifices time, and we need to bring forward the development,” he said. “If we went for a technical solution, it risks a lose-lose situation.”
New World, which is owned by the Cheng family through private holding company Chow Tai Fook Enterprises, announced on Wednesday that it would return the project to the authority by surrendering the infrastructure.
As part of the move, the developer will pay a HK$2.3 billion (US$293 million) break-up fee, spending HK$1.05 billion to complete the remaining works and provide agreed services, and offering a HK$1 option to buy the company’s shares.
“The whole package represents the biggest efforts of the major shareholder [of New World],” Lee said. “We have tried to maximise what we get. The option is a bonus.”
The option for the authority to buy 750 million New World shares also came with a string of conditions that have raised questions about its feasibility.




Under the conditions, the authority can only exercise the option within three years and must buy the shares in one go.
When it buys the shares, it cannot breach any bank covenants and cannot exceed the controlling shareholder’s interest. The authority would also be required to hold onto its stake in the company until September 2032.
The 750 million shares already represent 29.8 per cent of New World’s total issued share capital of 2.52 billion shares.
Chow Tai Fook Enterprises holds roughly a 45 per cent stake in New World and has indicated it intends to maintain its control of the developer.
The exercise price of the option will be HK$2.25 billion, or HK$3 per share – nearly a 50 per cent discount to Friday’s closing price of HK$5.82.
“New World will have a series of movements to follow,” Lee said without elaboration.
The developer has been offloading assets and refinancing capital to cut debt after a liquidity crisis emerged in 2023. As of June 30 this year, its total debts stood at HK$143.3 billion and its net debt was HK$126.3 billion.
The terminated contract was signed by New World in 2018 and was originally supposed to end in 2066.
The termination has attracted controversy as the move means the authority will give up its entitlement to receive 20 per cent of guaranteed rent or revenue rent, depending on whichever was higher, of the gross revenue from 11 Skies from 2027 to 2066.
The handover is due to be completed by April next year.
The 11 Skies project was intended to complement the authority’s goal of developing Skytopia, a HK$100 billion landmark surrounding Hong Kong International Airport, featuring commerce, culture, leisure and entertainment elements.

Cissy Chan Ching-sze, the authority’s executive director for commercial, said 11 Skies would be renamed soon and given a new identity before management hunted for investors and tenants.
“It will no longer be a mall,” she said. “It will be an entertainment hub.”
Originally, the HK$20 billion 11 Skies development was expected to include three grade A office towers totalling 52,955 square metres (570,000 square feet), and about 247,000 square metres of retail and dining space, representing 70 per cent of the entire project.
In May, the South China Morning Post reported that signs had emerged of the authority having regained control of the project.
In the first half of this year, the company wrote off HK$18.32 billion in net impairment losses and provisions on 11 Skies, following HK$2.7 billion in the same period in 2025.
Chan said some spaces in one of the office towers had been leased, while the other two were pending tenant recruitment.
“We aim to attract companies that organise exhibitions to move from Wan Chai to leverage more exhibitions to be held at AsiaWorld-Expo,” she said, adding that other potential tenants include private wealth and insurance companies.
The retail and dining spaces were repurposed as a destination for entertainment, wellness and experiences.
She cited restaurants offering jet-fresh seafood, carting and pet-friendly areas and spaces dedicated to visitors’ experiences as examples.
Chan said key components of Skytopia would be completed in 2028.
These include most parts of 11 Skies, an autonomous transport system that connects the Hong Kong checkpoint of the Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macau Bridge with Tung Chung MTR station, a 12,000 square metres waterfront piazza, a water recreation area and the expansion of nearby facilities at AsiaWorld-Expo.
AsiaWorld-Expo will add 100,000 square metres of exhibition space and a 20,000-seat super arena for concerts and other events.
Chan added that a section of the yacht bay berthing facilities was also expected to be ready for use in 2028.

data.title: China’s buying spree in ASML DUV gear prompts US calls for total export ban
data.description:
Chinese semiconductor plants amassed hundreds of immersion lithography machines worth billions of dollars in recent years, according to former US officials, who urged Washington and its allies to shut down further exports.
Chinese-owned fabs had acquired an estimated 343 immersion deep ultraviolet (DUV) lithography systems by early 2026, said a report published in late September by the Centre for Technology & Statecraft (CTS), a Washington research group established in August.
Co-authored by former US export control official Nicholas Brown and Saif Khan, a former White House and commerce department technology policy adviser, the study adds fresh data to the debate in Washington over whether Western allies should impose a total blockade on immersion DUV tools bound for China.
Blocked from buying Dutch toolmaker ASML’s most advanced extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography tools, Chinese chipmakers have leaned heavily on immersion DUV systems – some models of which remain exempt from Western export bans – to produce sophisticated semiconductors.
The report estimated that about 270 of the machines acquired by Chinese-owned plants were ASML’s Twinscan NXT:1980i immersion DUV systems.
Though technically behind EUV, these tools can be adapted to manufacture 7-nanometre-class logic chips and advanced memory for artificial intelligence processors, including Huawei Technologies’ Ascend series, the authors said.
Chinese fabs spent over US$13 billion acquiring about 90 NXT:1980i machines in 2024 and another 89 in 2025, according to the report.
The purported buying spree is reflected in ASML’s financial disclosures. China accounted for 41 per cent of the Dutch firm’s net system sales by shipment destination in 2024 and 33 per cent in 2025.

Sales to China have since moderated, dropping to 19 per cent of ASML’s total in the first quarter of 2026 and 14 per cent in the second. ASML previously said that its high level of 2024 shipments was partly driven by fulfilling backlogged orders delayed by earlier supply chain constraints.
The Netherlands began requiring export licences for ASML’s NXT:2000i and more advanced immersion DUV systems in September 2023. Those models have since been effectively barred from China. It extended the licence requirement to the NXT:1980i a year later, but shipments of that model can still be approved case by case.
The report argued that this approach left a major loophole, warning that even tools sold for mature chipmaking nodes can be repurposed or relocated to advanced production lines.
To close the loophole, the authors recommended a complete China-wide ban on all immersion DUV equipment, alongside restrictions on replacement parts and servicing at advanced facilities. They suggested Washington coordinate with the Netherlands or unilaterally extend American export rules to foreign-made systems using US tech.
The push aligns with growing pressure in US Congress.
The bipartisan Match Act, introduced in April, seeks China-wide restrictions on sales and servicing for chipmaking equipment that China cannot easily manufacture at home – explicitly targeting immersion DUV tools. Senators renewed calls for its passage in September, and Khan publicly endorsed the bill earlier this year.
While cut-offs would have little immediate impact because Chinese fabs have already built up an inventory of imported tools, the authors argued that the long-term difference would be substantial.
Under the study’s most expansive theoretical projection, if China overcame other chipmaking bottlenecks and continued importing about 90 NXT:1980i systems a year, its DUV fleet could support an annual output of up to 434 million AI chips equivalent to Nvidia’s H100 by 2035. Halting new imports in 2027 would cap that ceiling at 153 million units, it said.

data.title: MTR Corp pays out HK$2.25 billion for high-speed rail construction delays
data.description:
The MTR Corporation will hand over HK$2.25 billion (US$287 million) to the Hong Kong government as a one-off settlement for the delayed completion of the high-speed rail line, while reaching a consensus to avoid a payout over hurdles affecting the Sha Tin to Central Link.
While the transport firm oversaw the design, construction, testing, and operation of the two projects, both are owned by the government and involved public funds.
Under the arrangements announced on Friday, the MTR Corp will pay the government, its majority shareholder, HK$2.25 billion for the delay to the commencement of the 26km (16.1-mile) local section of the cross-border High Speed Rail, which was completed in 2018.
But the MTR Corp and authorities also agreed not to pursue further claims over the Sha Tin to Central Link, as the rail firm had shouldered HK$2.8 billion in extra costs to address quality issues and delays.
The project, which connects Admiralty MTR station to stops at the Hong Kong-mainland Chinese border, was completed in 2022 after repeated delays and a scandal over the substandard construction of Hung Hom station.
“The government has been following up in a serious, rigorous and professional manner with [the MTR Corp] on its responsibilities as the project manager in respect of programme delays in the construction of the [high-speed rail and Shatin to Central Link] projects, in order to safeguard the legitimate interests of the government and the public,” the Transport and Logistics Bureau said.
A government spokesman said both parties had learned lessons from the delays and implemented a series of mechanisms to strengthen railway project governance, supervision and cost control.
Jeny Yeung Mei-chun, CEO of the MTR Corp, said the firm had encountered significant difficulties during the course of construction.
“The corporation has drawn lessons from the two projects and conducted reviews and rigorous follow-up in light of their specific circumstances,” she said.
“Drawing on our extensive experience in railway construction and operations, we will continue to provide the railway infrastructure critical to Hong Kong’s future development and support the city’s long-term sustainable growth.”

data.title: Legislators urge broader cooling-off law after abrupt Hotstone Yoga closure
data.description:
Hong Kong lawmakers have urged the government to widen the scope of a proposed statutory cooling-off law to cover more types of wellness market trends after the abrupt shutdown of the Hotstone Yoga chain, as claimed financial losses by customers rose to HK$3.9 million (US$497,030).
Their calls followed the government’s commitment to introduce a bill in the Legislative Council in the first half of next year that would establish a statutory cooling-off period for prepaid fitness and beauty contracts.
However, lawmakers said on Friday that the current proposals were too narrowly focused on fitness centres and beauty parlours, leaving consumers unprotected against evolving wellness trends.
Lawmaker Jeff Yiu Ming said the legislation needed to keep pace with shifting market trends, pointing out that fitness offerings now included kickboxing, Pilates and yoga.
“The government might need to define statutory terms with precision to ensure all emerging wellness concepts fall within the law’s purview,” he said.
Secretary for Commerce and Economic Development Algernon Yau Ying-wah previously said authorities hoped to introduce the amendment bill to Legco in the first half of 2027, although timing remained subject to other agenda priorities.
The administration has proposed rolling out a statutory seven-day cooling-off period and a 14-day refund window for prepaid beauty and fitness contracts. It has also suggested exempting lower-value contracts to minimise disruption, with the threshold ranging from HK$3,000 (US$382) to HK$15,000 or above.
Lawmaker Bill Tang Ka-piu also urged the government to expand the scope of the legal framework to protect the rights of the public.
“We need a clear overarching legal framework covering all business-to-customer prepaid contracts for future services across all sectors,” he said.

Tang added that while government officials assured him that centres offering both yoga and general fitness classes would fall within the scope of the statutory cooling-off period, real-world market operations presented numerous grey areas.
Without explicit statutory coverage, “everyday consumers without a legal background are easily left in the dark,” he warned, acknowledging that broader restrictions would likely face pushback from the business sector.
A customer who identified herself only as Chan earlier told the South China Morning Post that she understood at least 500 customers had suffered financial losses due to the abrupt closure of Hotstone Yoga.
A closure notice, issued by law firm Cheung & Co and posted outside the studios, stated the chain was shutting down after careful consideration due to “business operations and other actual circumstances.”
It stated the company would cease operations at the end of regular business hours on Wednesday and included an email address for parties holding “rights, debts or other claims against Hotstone” to submit documents.
The notice added that affected staff could inquire with the relevant government departments about their rights and file related applications, and Hotstone would provide the necessary documents and information “where reasonably practicable” to facilitate procedures.
The company said it would pay outstanding wages for September and refund class fees from that month by October 5.
Most of Hotstone’s social media pages were disabled by Thursday afternoon.
According to its Threads account, the business operated for 10 years and had studios in Central, Causeway Bay, Aberdeen, Jordan, Tsuen Wan, Sha Tin and Kwun Tong.
It also claimed to be the first studio in Hong Kong to provide hot stone yoga sessions, stating it employed more than 100 veteran instructors to teach yoga, stretching, dance and gym classes.
The Consumer Council said that as of Friday 5pm, it had received 286 complaints related to the chain’s closure involving claimed losses of HK$3,909,444.
Police said they had received multiple reports since October 1 from individuals who claimed to have purchased class packages at a local yoga centre that abruptly closed.
The case will be referred to relevant departments for follow-up.
